title: and but or so because
subtitle: joining two sentences
summary: Join two short sentences into one with and, but, or, so and because.

lesson.heading: Joining two sentences
lesson.text: We use **and**, **but**, **or**, **so** and **because** to join two sentences. They make one longer sentence from two shorter ones.

examples.text: The car stopped. + The driver got out.
The car stopped **and** the driver got out.

lesson.heading: and / but / or
lesson.text: **and** puts two things together, **but** shows a difference, and **or** gives a choice. When the person is the same in both parts, you do not need to say it again.

examples.text: We stayed at home **and** watched television.
examples.note: You do not need to repeat *we*.

examples.text: My sister is married **and** lives in London.
He doesn't like her, **and** she doesn't like him.
I bought a newspaper, **but** I didn't read it.
It's a nice house, **but** it hasn't got a garden.
Do you want to go out, **or** are you too tired?

lesson.heading: Lists
lesson.text: In a list we use commas (,) and we put **and** before the last thing.

examples.text: I got home, had something to eat, sat down in an armchair **and** fell asleep.
Karen is at work, Sue has gone shopping **and** Chris is playing football.

lesson.heading: so and because

left.label: so - the result
left.text: After so we say what happened because of the first part.
examples: It was very hot, **so** I opened the window.
Joe does a lot of sport, **so** he's very fit.
They don't like travelling, **so** they haven't been to many places.

right.label: because - the reason
examples: I opened the window **because** it was very hot.
Joe can't come to the party **because** he's going away.
Lisa is hungry **because** she didn't have breakfast.

lesson.note: **Because** is also possible at the beginning: *Because it was very hot, I opened the window.*

lesson.heading: Which word?
rows: The car stopped **and** the driver got out.
I bought a newspaper, **but** I didn't read it.
Do you want to go out, **or** are you too tired?
It was very hot, **so** I opened the window.
I opened the window **because** it was very hot.

lesson.heading: More than one joining word
lesson.text: One long sentence can have two of these words.

examples.text: It was late **and** I was tired, **so** I went to bed.
I always enjoy visiting London, **but** I wouldn't like to live there **because** it's too big.

exercises.prompt: I bought a newspaper, ___ I didn't read it.
exercises.explanation: but shows a difference between the two parts.

exercises.prompt: I opened the window ___ it was very hot.
exercises.explanation: The second part gives the reason, so we use because.

exercises.prompt: Joe does a lot of sport, ___ he's very fit.
exercises.explanation: The second part is the result, so we use so.

exercises.statement: The car stopped and the driver got out.
exercises.explanation: Correct. and joins the two sentences into one.

exercises.prompt: Which word joins each pair of sentences: so or because?

items.text: Joe does a lot of sport. He's very fit.
They don't like travelling. They haven't been to many places.
It was late and I was tired. I went to bed.
Joe can't come to the party. He's going away.
Lisa is hungry. She didn't have breakfast.
I opened the window. It was very hot.

exercises.prompt: Join two sentences: I went to the window. I looked out.
exercises.answer: I went to the window and looked out.
exercises.explanation: The person is the same, so you do not repeat I after and.

exercises.prompt: Match each beginning with the right ending.

pairs.right: because there was a lot of traffic.

pairs.left: It was late and I was tired,

exercises.prompt: I usually drive to work, ___ I went by bus this morning.
exercises.explanation: This morning was different from usual, so we use but.

exercises.prompt: Join two sentences: I wanted to phone you. I didn't have your number.
exercises.answer: I wanted to phone you, but I didn't have your number.
exercises.explanation: but shows the difference between what you wanted and what happened.

exercises.statement: I always enjoy visiting London, so I wouldn't like to live there.
exercises.explanation: I always enjoy visiting London, but I wouldn't like to live there because it's too big.

exercises.prompt: Join two sentences: Do you want me to come with you? Shall I wait here?
words: Do you want me to come with you,
exercises.answer: Do you want me to come with you, or shall I wait here?
exercises.explanation: or gives the other person a choice.

exercises.prompt: Join two sentences: I jumped into the river. I swam to the other side.
exercises.answer: I jumped into the river and swam to the other side.
exercises.explanation: The person is the same in both parts, so I is not repeated after and.
